implementation_notes: ScalaMock generates doubles for traits and classes (including final ones on Scala 3) through a macro-based MockFactory: mock[Service].getUserName.expects(42).returns("John") programmes the expectation, stub[T] is the lenient variant for calls that only need canned answers, and verification is explicit with (service.getUserName _).verify(42).once(). It integrates with ScalaTest, specs2, ZIO Test and cats-effect, and its stubs module verifies after the fact through .calls/.times, so a hand-written dummy is only needed where macros are unacceptable.
code_sketch:
class OrderSpec extends AnyFlatSpec with MockFactory:
  "an order" should "remove stock" in:
    val warehouse = mock[Warehouse]
    (warehouse.hasInventory _).expects("Talisker", 50).returns(true)
    (warehouse.remove _).expects("Talisker", 50).returns(true)

    assert(Order("Talisker", 50).fill(warehouse))
    (warehouse.remove _).verify("Talisker", 50).once()
pitfalls: mock[T] is strict - an unexpected call fails immediately - while stub[T] returns defaults; confusing the two produces either noisy failures or silently passing tests.
Expectation cardinality defaults to a single call unless it is widened explicitly, so a collaborator invoked in a loop fails classification until .repeat/.anyNumberOfTimes says otherwise.
Macro mocking is platform-specific: Scala 3 covers JVM, JS and Native, while 2.12/2.13 only exist for JVM and JS, so a cross-built module needs the matching scalamock artifact.
